newsitem.title: ITALY: Cargo plane crashes in Italian village, 4 dead.
newsitem.headline: Cargo plane crashes in Italian village, 4 dead.

text.p: A Russian Antonov cargo plane crashed into a village while trying to land at Turin airport in northwest Italy on Tuesday, ploughing through farmhouses and killing at least four people. More than 20 on board survived.
"I heard a dull thud, I went out and I saw the tail of the plane sticking out of a house," said Alessandro Renzi, who lives close to the scene of the accident.
"Then I saw two men come out of the plane's tail and walk towards me in a confused state asking me in English to call an ambulance," Renzi told Reuters.

The pilot and another crew member were killed in the crash in the village of San Francesco al Campo as the jet-powered Antonov 124 with 23 people on board came in to land on a flight from Moscow, an official at the local prefecture said.

Two villagers were also killed when they were buried in rubble as the plane sliced through buildings before coming to rest less than a kilometre (half a mile) from Turin's Caselle airport. Two other villagers were hurt.

Rescue workers said 13 crew members were being treated for injuries in hospitals in the Turin area while another eight escaped unhurt from the crash. All on board the aircraft were believed to be Russians.

The plane was owned by the Moscow-based Ayaks Cargo Airlines, a company spokesman in Britain said. It was leased to the Russian airline Aeroflot, which provided the crew, and chartered by British air cargo broker Aviation Consultants, the spokesman said.
The Antonov was built in 1993 and was insured for $10 million, an insurance broker in London said.
After the pilot apparently aborted a first attempt to land, the plane seemed to stall as it prepared to make a fresh approach, the prefecture official said.
The cause of the crash was not immediately clear but a fire brigade spokesman in Rome said pilot error may have played a part. "It appears there was an error in the landing operation."
Visibility was believed to be good although it was raining at the time the plane came down, the spokesman said.
The airport was closed for several hours after the accident.
The plane was to have picked up a consignment of luxury cars before flying to the Gulf state of Sharjah and on to Brunei in the Far East.
The plane struck two houses before smashing into a farm building and coming to a halt on a road close to a cemetery in the village outside Turin.
Firemen said later they had feared the plane, which still had a large amount of fuel in its tanks, might blow up.
Italian television showed images of the mangled wreckage of the plane covered in rubble. Splintered pieces of the plane's undercarriage were seen lodged in a nearby barn.
